pronunciation.note: Cáishén is Tier 1 because the name is natively written in Chinese characters (財神) — a script with no ASCII equivalent — and the tone-marked pinyin preserves the pronunciation that plain romanization flattens.

domains.title: Wealth
domains.subtitle: Wealth, Prosperity, New Year
domains.lead: Cáishén (財神, 'God of Wealth') is less a single god than an office, filled across the centuries by a canonized marshal, a heartless minister, and an honest merchant. He presides over trade, treasure, and the New Year, when every household races to be the first to welcome him.

cards.name: Marshal Zhao
cards.desc: Zhao Gongming: black tiger, iron whip, gold ingot — the Martial God of Wealth canonized in the Fengshen Yanyi.

cards.name: The Civil God
cards.desc: Bi Gan, the Shang minister whose heart King Zhou cut out; without a heart, he cannot be greedy, so merchants trust him.

cards.name: Welcoming the God
cards.desc: On the fifth day of the New Year, businesses reopen with firecrackers to be first to receive him.

cards.name: The Five Paths
cards.desc: Worshipped in sets of five — the Five Gods of Wealth, bringing fortune from every direction of the compass.

symbols.name: The gold ingot (yuanbao)
symbols.meaning: The boat-shaped silver-gold ingot held by every avatar of Cáishén — wealth made visible and graspable.

symbols.name: The black tiger
symbols.meaning: Marshal Zhao's mount; the tiger that can carry wealth away as easily as it brings it.

symbols.name: The iron whip
symbols.meaning: Zhao Gongming's weapon, disciplining the pursuit of riches — wealth taken unjustly is wealth reclaimed.

symbols.name: The ruyi scepter
symbols.meaning: 'As you wish' — the wish-granting wand of the Civil God of Wealth.

symbols.name: The account book
symbols.meaning: The ledger in which the god's office records each household's fortune for the coming year.

symbols.name: The Five Paths
symbols.meaning: Five directional gods of wealth — east, south, west, north, and center — for fortune has a road from every quarter.

mythology.lead: Cáishén's mythology is young and openly composite. The cult is a Song-dynasty growth over older roots, and every avatar brings his own story: a Ming novel supplies the marshal, a Han historian the heartless minister, merchants the retired sage. The tradition never pretends otherwise — and its honesty is part of its power.

myths.title: One Office, Many Gods
myths.text: The two characters 財神 simply mean 'god of wealth' — a title, not a personal name, and the tradition treats it that way. There is no canonical birth-story of Cáishén; instead, the office has been filled, again and again, by figures the culture wished to honor: a loyal minister, a canonized marshal, an honest merchant, even the red-faced war-god Guan Yu in some regions. The clearest early attestations belong to the Song dynasty (960–1279), when China's commercial revolution made wealth a god worth petitioning; the Ming-era compendium Santjiao soushen daquan and the novel Fengshen Yanyi then fixed the cast of avatars. The sources disagree openly about who 'really' holds the office — which is the honest thing for a god of fortune, since every trade, region, and dynasty wants to claim him. A god with many faces is a god owned by many classes; Cáishén's multiplicity is the theology of a civilization that decided prosperity itself was divine.

myths.title: Zhao Gongming on the Black Tiger
myths.text: The fullest avatar-story comes from the Ming novel Fengshen Yanyi (Investiture of the Gods). During the fall of the Shang dynasty, Zhao Gongming, a hermit of Mount Emei, comes down to aid the doomed house with his black tiger, his iron whip, and his magic pearls; battle after battle turns on his power, until Jiang Ziya's side breaks him with Lu Ya's sorcery — an effigy of straw pierced by arrows. When the war ends and the fallen are canonized, Jiang Ziya invests the dead marshal as the God of Wealth, true lord of the dragon-tiger altar, mounted on his tiger, whip in hand, gold ingot ready — with four assistant deities who manage the welcoming of treasure, the gathering of valuables, the inviting of wealth, and the profiting of markets. The novel turns fortune into a bureaucracy: wealth flows not from luck but from an office, staffed, audited, and answerable — a very Chinese answer to the oldest of prayers.

myths.title: Bi Gan's Missing Heart
myths.text: The civil face of the god descends from an atrocity recorded by Sima Qian in the Shiji (c. 90 BCE, 'Basic Annals of Yin'). Bi Gan, uncle and chief minister of King Zhou of Shang, remonstrated against the tyrant's cruelties until the king, goaded on by his favorite Daji, ordered the minister's heart cut out — to test the old claim that a sage's heart has seven openings. Because Bi Gan died heartless, later tradition reasoned, he is beyond greed: no bribe reaches a god who has no heart to desire one. He became the Civil God of Wealth, the form merchants and bankers trust, usually shown in an official's robes holding a ruyi scepter and a scroll. The logic is ruthless and perfectly practical: the only trustworthy custodian of wealth is the man whose desire for it has been surgically removed — a parable about greed built on a mutilation, and one of the darkest etiologies any god carries.

myths.title: Fan Li, Thrice Rich
myths.text: A third avatar rises from honest trade. Fan Li — again from Sima Qian — was the strategist who destroyed the rival state of Wu and saved Yue, then refused office and reward, changed his name, and took to commerce; he grew rich, gave it all away, started over, and did this three times, dying in comfort at last under the name Tao Zhu Gong. Merchants made him Cáishén because his fortune was a skill, not a windfall, and because he spent as brilliantly as he earned. Where Bi Gan's wealth is incorruptible and Zhao's is martial, Fan Li's is mercantile: prosperity as craft plus generosity. The choice of a retired official for the marketplace form of the god says something careful about Chinese commerce — that it does not entirely trust itself, and wants its wealth-god to be a man who walked away from power, made money in the open, and let it go.

myths.title: Welcoming Cáishén
myths.text: The living myth is a calendar custom. On the fifth day of the first lunar month — po wu, 'breaking the five' — Cáishén makes his annual circuit, and every shop and household races to be the first to welcome him. At midnight before, firecrackers tear the dark open; the paper icon that watched over the old year is burned to send the god on his way; dumplings are eaten 'to pinch the villain's mouth' shut. The folk tale behind the noise tells of a merchant so poor his only offering was a single stick of incense — and the god, pleased by the welcome and not the wealth, made his fortune. Businesses time their reopening to the day; the first trade of the year is literally kept by the god's schedule. It is the theology of a merchant culture in one image: fortune is real, it circulates, and it favors the one who stays up past midnight, firecracker in hand, at the door to receive it.

lore.syncretism: Cáishén was assembled by borrowing. The novel's machinery of canonization is Daoist — Jiang Ziya's investiture lists are pure Daoist pantheon-building, and temple practice couches the god in Daoist liturgy. From Buddhism came wealth-deities the Tang already naturalized: Vaiśravaṇa (Bishamonten), the northern king and treasure-guardian, and Jambhala in the Tibetan and Mongolian lands. The closest foreign counterpart is Japan's Daikokuten — Mahākāla turned money-god, often fused with Ōkuninushi — one of the Seven Gods of Fortune. Vietnam keeps Thần Tài beside the earth-god Ông Địa on every family altar, and Hong Kong's banks host the lion dance at New Year. Across the Sinosphere, wealth was the one god every household kept — and each culture built its own face for him.
lore.culturalLegacy: At Lunar New Year, Cáishén is the busiest god alive. The fifth-day welcome, the firecrackers, the reopened shops, the paper icons, and the greeting Gong Xi Fa Cai — 'wishing you prosperity' — all run on his calendar, from Harbin to Singapore to San Francisco. Hong Kong's markets watch the god's day; diaspora restaurants keep his altar by the register, oranges and gold ingots before the red-faced image. The digital age has not displaced him but multiplied his mediums: apps send red envelopes, and his portrait rides phone wallpapers through the New Year. A god minted by Song-dynasty commerce now banks the hopes of two billion people a year — the largest recurring act of popular worship on earth.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Cáishén is a mirror. A civilization's wealth-god shows what that civilization thinks wealth is: the Greeks had Ploutos, a blind boy; Rome had Fortuna, a wheel; China built a bureaucracy. Marshal Zhao on his tiger says wealth has teeth; Bi Gan's missing heart says wealth corrupts; Fan Li's three fortunes say wealth is a craft; the four assistants — welcome treasure, gather valuables, invite wealth, profit the market — say it is, above all, an office with paperwork.

There is wisdom in the composite. No single story could carry the whole moral weight of money, so the tradition carries it by committee and lets each petitioner choose the face that fits. And the New Year custom keeps the deepest truth: fortune circulates. The god who arrives at midnight, received with noise and incense by whoever stays at the door, is a theology of readiness — prosperity favors the one awake to welcome it. That is not superstition. It is a culture's entire theory of prosperity, printed on red paper and burned, year after year, to send it on its rounds.

lore.archaeology: The material record of Cáishén is popular, mass-produced, and deliberately ephemeral — which is itself testimony. Late-imperial woodblock New Year prints (nianhua) from Yangliuqing (Tianjin), Taohuawu (Suzhou), and Mianzhu (Sichuan) turned out hundreds of thousands of red-and-gold god-images each winter, to be pasted above doorways and burned in the fourth-night send-off. The Yuan–Ming god-compendium Santjiao soushen daquan reached households in cheap woodblock editions that carried the mythology to the non-literate. Wealth-god shrines stand in guild halls and temples across the Sinosphere, usually flanked by his assistants with the tiger at his feet; paper and porcelain icons still sit on shop altars everywhere, replaced annually — wealth itself made a renewable rite.
